title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 18
paragraphs: From the moment he received this news until the end of the campaign, all of Kutuzov's energy was directed toward restraining his troops—by authority, by cunning, and by pleading—from useless attacks, maneuvers, and clashes with the dying enemy. Dokhturov went to Malo-Yaroslavets, but Kutuzov lingered with the main army and gave orders for the evacuation of Kaluga—a retreat beyond that town seemed entirely possible to him.
Everywhere Kutuzov retreated, but the enemy, without waiting for his retreat, fled in the opposite direction.

Napoleon's historians describe his skillful maneuvers at Tarutino and Malo-Yaroslavets and speculate about what might have happened if Napoleon had managed to reach the rich southern provinces in time.

But setting aside the fact that nothing prevented him from advancing south (the Russian army wasn't blocking his way), the historians forget that nothing could have saved his army, because it already carried within itself the seeds of inevitable destruction. How could that army—which had found abundant supplies in Moscow and trampled them underfoot instead of preserving them, and which on arriving at Smolensk had looted provisions instead of storing them—how could such an army recover in Kaluga province, inhabited by the same kind of Russians who lived in Moscow, where fire had the same ability to consume whatever was set ablaze?
That army could not recover anywhere. Since the Battle of Borodino and the pillaging of Moscow, it had carried within itself the chemical elements of its own dissolution.

The members of what had once been an army—Napoleon himself and all his soldiers—fled without knowing where, each concerned only with escaping as quickly as possible from a situation whose hopelessness they all more or less vaguely sensed.

So at the council at Malo-Yaroslavets, when the generals pretended to deliberate and offered various opinions, all mouths were shut by the opinion of the plain-spoken soldier Mouton, who spoke last and said what they all felt: the only thing to do was get away as fast as possible. And no one—not even Napoleon—could argue against that truth they all recognized.

But though everyone realized they had to retreat, there remained a feeling of shame at admitting they had to flee. An outside jolt was needed to overcome that shame, and it came right on time. The French called it 'the Emperor's hurrah.'

The day after the council at Malo-Yaroslavets, Napoleon rode out early among the lines of his army with his marshals and escort, ostensibly to inspect the troops and the scene of the recent and upcoming battle. Some Cossacks out looking for plunder ran into the Emperor and very nearly captured him. What saved Napoleon wasn't the strength of his forces but the very thing that was destroying the French army: the lure of loot. The Cossacks went after the plunder, just as they had at Tarutino, leaving the men behind. Ignoring Napoleon, they chased the booty, and Napoleon managed to escape.

When 'the children of the Don' could so easily have captured the Emperor himself in the midst of his army, it was clear there was nothing to do but flee as fast as possible along the nearest, most familiar road. Napoleon, with his forty-year-old stomach, understood the hint. No longer feeling his former agility and boldness, and shaken by the fright the Cossacks had given him, he immediately agreed with Mouton and issued orders—as the historians tell us—to retreat along the Smolensk road.

That Napoleon agreed with Mouton, and that the army retreated, doesn't prove that Napoleon caused it to retreat. Rather, the forces influencing the entire army and directing it along the Mozhaysk (that is, the Smolensk) road were simultaneously acting on him as well.
